input: Interview my grandmother about her childhood memories

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Childhood memories could mean a specific era, place, or theme (e.g. wartime, family traditions, school life) — knowing the focus shapes which questions to prepare.
Whether this is just for the user personally, or meant to be shared with the wider family, changes the depth, tone, and formality of the interview.
Whether the interview is in-person, over a video call, or via written exchange affects how it is conducted and what tools are needed.
The grandmother's energy, health, or availability may limit session length or require the interview to be broken into multiple sittings.
The output format — audio recording, video, written transcript, or a family memoir — determines what equipment or tools are needed and how to prepare.
Whether the tone should be casual and conversational or structured and documentary-style affects how questions are written and how the user guides the discussion.
Knowing what 'done well' looks like — a full life-story archive vs. a single cherished story to share at a family event — sets the right level of effort and scope.

gold.taskTitle: Interview Grandmother About Her Childhood Memories
gold.taskDescription: Conduct a meaningful interview with the user's grandmother to capture her childhood memories in some lasting or useful form.

questions.title: What specific themes or eras should the interview focus on?
questions.description: Determine whether the interview covers a broad sweep of childhood or zooms into specific topics like family traditions, school, a particular place, or a historical period.

questions.title: Who is the intended audience for these captured memories?
questions.description: Clarify whether the interview is a private keepsake for the user, a gift for immediate family, or something to be shared across a wider family circle or community.

questions.title: Will the interview happen in person or remotely?
questions.description: Establish the setting — a face-to-face visit, a video call, or an asynchronous written exchange — as this directly shapes the preparation and tools required.

questions.title: How much time can your grandmother comfortably give?
questions.description: Understand any time or energy constraints on the grandmother's side so the session length and number of sittings can be planned appropriately.

questions.title: How do you want to record or preserve the interview?
questions.description: Decide on the output format — audio recording, video, written notes, a typed transcript, or a printed booklet — to determine what equipment or apps are needed.

questions.title: Should the conversation feel casual or structured and documentary-style?
questions.description: Establish the desired tone so interview questions can be written to feel natural and comfortable for the grandmother, or more thorough and methodical if needed.

questions.title: What would make this interview feel truly complete or successful?
questions.description: Define the end goal — for example, one powerful story to share at a family event, a full archive of memories, or a written chapter in a family history project.
